title: Alert-budget metrics and a time-and-group split
request: Report what an analyst plans with: recall and precision within the alerts the team can review, and a split that keeps both time order and entities apart instead of silently dropping the group.
spec: recall_at_budget, precision_at_budget and AP lift in the binary metrics; Solution.alert_budget; the budget metric selectable as primary; a time-and-group split (forward folds, an entity seen in training removed from the later test fold, the number removed reported); precision a lower bound with partial labels. Done when the metrics match hand-computed values, the split never puts an entity on both sides, and the replica's final stage reports recall at the budget with a cluster-bootstrap interval.
plan: Read how the engine builds its splits and metrics today.
Add runner.budget_metrics and pass the budget through compute_metrics and the bootstrap.
Add split strategy time_group in expansion/datasets.py: forward folds with seen entities removed and the removal reported, refused with a reason when almost every entity recurs.
Add the metric's code to the exported notebook, then remove the 15.3 marker from the acceptance test.
Test the metrics against hand-computed values and the split for entity overlap; fix the Step 2 review's findings.

decisions.decision: The time-and-group split refuses with a reason rather than drop either constraint.
decisions.why: Dropping the group lets entities leak; dropping time hides drift. When almost every entity recurs, no honest forward test exists, and saying so is better than a quiet compromise.

decisions.decision: The plan proposes the time-and-group split only when the overlap allows it; otherwise it groups by the entity and states the drift.
decisions.why: A plan that asks for a split the engine must refuse produces a project that cannot run.

decisions.decision: The budget is a share of rows the team can review.
decisions.why: An analyst plans with 'about 70 a day', which becomes a share of the scored rows.

change: runner.budget_metrics (recall, precision and alerts at the budget, AP lift), Solution.alert_budget, recall_at_budget as a primary metric, its cluster-bootstrap interval in the final stage, split time_group in datasets.py, the plan's RECURRING check before proposing it, the metric in the exported notebook; tests in tests/test_labels.py.

findings.defect: The recall-at-budget interval was biased low.
findings.scenario: In a cluster bootstrap over a few fraud bikers, many resamples hold no positive; budget_metric_fn returned 0.0 for them, pulling the interval's low end to 0.
findings.cause: A resample without a positive was scored as a total miss instead of as saying nothing.
findings.fix: Return NaN for such a draw; bootstrap_ci already drops non-finite values.
findings.impact: With only a few fraud bikers, the reported interval for recall at the budget would start near zero whatever the model did, so a team would read a useful model as possibly worthless and could reject it on an artefact of the bootstrap.

findings.defect: An adopted plan could ask for a split the engine then refuses, so every stage failed.
findings.scenario: dclab_core.plan proposed time_and_group from drift plus repeated entities without checking their overlap; with recurring customers fewer than about 10% of later rows remain once seen entities are removed, the new split refuses, and the project cannot run.
findings.cause: The plan and the split applied different conditions.
findings.fix: The plan reads the share of later rows that belong to entities seen earlier; at 90% or more it groups by the entity, states the drift, and lists the time-and-group split as an alternative with the share it would remove.
findings.impact: A person who adopted DCLab's own plan on a table of recurring customers would get a project in which every stage failed: the plan asked for a split the engine then refused, and the person had followed the advice exactly.
alternatives: Let the engine fall back to another split and state it: set aside for checking the overlap in the plan, so the plan never proposes a split that cannot run and shows the share of rows it would remove.

outcome: Done: budget metrics checked by hand, a time-and-entity split that never puts an entity on both sides and refuses when it cannot test, recall at the budget with a cluster-bootstrap interval in the replica's final stage.
lessons: A resample with no positive carries no information about recall: drop it, never score it 0.
A planner and an executor must share the condition that decides whether a choice can run.
risks: A split that drops the group when time order is chosen lets one entity sit on both sides; time and entity must both hold, with the rows removed reported.
Removing entities seen in training can leave a test fold too small to test; the split must refuse then, and the plan must not propose it.
A cluster bootstrap over a few positive entities produces many resamples with no positive; how they are scored biases the interval.
With partial labels, precision at the budget is only a lower bound and must be reported as one.
Metrics at a budget must match hand-computed values, including ties at the budget's edge.
